final_proof:
**Conventions and definitions.** Write $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\dots\}$ for the index set, matching the series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty v_n$. (If $\mathbb N$ is taken to start at $0$, the same argument works word for word with all partial sums starting at $n=0$.) Let $\|\cdot\|$ be the norm of $V$ and put
$$a_n := \|v_n\| \ge 0 \qquad (n\in\mathbb N).$$

For a finite set $F\subseteq\mathbb N$ let $s_F:=\sum_{n\in F} a_n$ (with $s_\varnothing=0$), and for $m\in\mathbb N$ let $S_m:=\sum_{n=1}^m a_n = s_{\{1,\dots,m\}}$.

We use the standard definitions:

* A generalized sum $\sum\{x_i : i\in I\}$ of elements of a normed space **converges to** $x$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite $F_0\subseteq I$ such that $\bigl\|\sum_{i\in F}x_i - x\bigr\|<\varepsilon$ for every finite $F$ with $F_0\subseteq F\subseteq I$. The generalized sum $\sum\{v_n : n\in\mathbb N\}$ is **absolutely net convergent to $r$** if the generalized sum $\sum\{\|v_n\| : n\in\mathbb N\}$ of real numbers converges to $r$.
* The series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty v_n$ is **absolutely convergent to $r$** if the real series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \|v_n\|$ converges to $r$, i.e. $S_m\to r$ as $m\to\infty$.

So we must prove:
$$\text{(1)}\ \ \forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists\text{ finite }F_0\ \forall\text{ finite }F\supseteq F_0:\ |s_F-r|<\varepsilon
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{(2)}\ \ S_m\to r .$$
(The completeness of $V$ plays no role. Only the fact that each $a_n\ge 0$ matters.)

**Two elementary facts.**

(a) *Monotonicity.* If $F\subseteq G$ are finite, then $s_G - s_F=\sum_{n\in G\setminus F}a_n\ge 0$, so $s_F\le s_G$. In particular $(S_m)$ is nondecreasing, and if $F\subseteq\{1,\dots,m\}$ then $s_F\le S_m$.

(b) *A nondecreasing convergent sequence is bounded above by its limit.* Suppose $S_m\to r$ and $S_k>r$ for some $k$. By (a), $S_m\ge S_k$ for all $m\ge k$, so $r=\lim_m S_m\ge S_k>r$, a contradiction. Hence $S_m\le r$ for all $m$.

**Proof of (1) $\Rightarrow$ (2).** Assume (1) and let $\varepsilon>0$. Choose a finite $F_0\subseteq\mathbb N$ as in (1), and let $m_0:=\max(F_0\cup\{1\})$ (this also covers $F_0=\varnothing$). For every $m\ge m_0$ the finite set $\{1,\dots,m\}$ contains $F_0$, so by (1)
$$|S_m-r| = |s_{\{1,\dots,m\}}-r|<\varepsilon .$$
Since $\varepsilon>0$ was arbitrary, $S_m\to r$, i.e. $\sum_{n=1}^\infty\|v_n\|=r$. This is (2).

**Proof of (2) $\Rightarrow$ (1).** Assume $S_m\to r$. By (b), $S_m\le r$ for all $m$. Let $\varepsilon>0$. Choose $M\in\mathbb N$ with $|S_M-r|<\varepsilon$. Together with $S_M\le r$ this gives
$$r-\varepsilon<S_M\le r .$$
Put $F_0:=\{1,\dots,M\}$, a finite set with $s_{F_0}=S_M$. Let $F\subseteq\mathbb N$ be any finite set with $F_0\subseteq F$, and let $m:=\max F$ (note $F\ne\varnothing$ since $M\in F_0\subseteq F$). Then $F_0\subseteq F\subseteq\{1,\dots,m\}$, so by (a) and (b)
$$r-\varepsilon< S_M = s_{F_0}\le s_F\le S_m\le r .$$
Hence $|s_F-r|<\varepsilon$ for every finite $F\supseteq F_0$. Since $\varepsilon>0$ was arbitrary, the generalized sum $\sum\{\|v_n\|:n\in\mathbb N\}$ converges to $r$. That is, $\sum\{v_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$ is absolutely net convergent to $r$, which is (1).

Both implications hold, so (1) and (2) are equivalent. $\blacksquare$
